All dried DA-polyesters were covered with aluminum foil and stored in a vacuum desiccator at room temperature.
Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra of the DA-polyesters were recorded using a Perkin– Elmer system 2000 FTIR spectrometer equipped with microscope and diamond press accessories.
All DA-polyesters were analyzed from 40 to 250°C under nitrogen purge at the heating rate of 10°C/min.
A film clamp and a single cantilever clamp were used to test solution-cast HT thin film and melt-processed OT(2) samples, respectively.
DA-polyesters were synthesized via interfacial condensation in an aqueous-toluene and had reasonably good yields except for HP and OT(2M).

It is thought that the condensation method has its advantages such as simplicity and relatively high yield, though DA-containing polymers may also be synthesized via other route like oxidative coupling.<sup>23,24</sup> This method is also more in line with the conventional polymerization and would enable other chemical manipulations such as copolymerization with conventional monomers.

FTIR spectra of the as-synthesised DA-polyesters HS, HI, HT, and OT(2) are shown in Figure 1.
For all aromatic DA-polyesters, the sharp and strong band at $7 3 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { \hat { - } \mathbf { 1 } }$is attributed to CH wagging vibrations of the benzene ring.
Raman spectroscopy is complementary to infrared spectroscopy, and is a better technique to detect the formation of the PDA chains and to investigate the factors that affect the crosspolymerization.
Raman spectra of as-synthesised DApolyesters of HS, HI, HT, and OT(2) are shown in Figure 2.
It is indicated that aliphatic DA-polyester HS is partially crosspolymerized during purification and upon storage.

This is clearly illustrated in Figure 2 that, in addition to the band of unreacted diacetylene $( { \mathrm { - } } \mathrm { C } { \equiv } \mathrm { C } { \mathrm { - } } \mathrm { C } { \equiv } \mathrm { C } { \mathrm { - } } )$at about $2 2 6 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$, bands of C'C and C|C vibration in polydiacetylene are also seen at 2106 and $1 5 0 7 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$.
The vibrational bands for polydiacetylene, however, were not detected in the as-synthesised aromatic DA-polyester HT, HI, and OT(2).
Figure 3 shows the Raman spectra of thermally treated DA-polyesters.
The aromatic DA-polyesters HI, HT, and OT(2) were isothermally treated in nitrogen at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for 45 h, while HS was treated for 15 h.
This indicated that most of the diacetylene units have crosspolymerized into polydiacetylene chains after the thermal treatment.

It is quite clear that the differences in molecular packing of the polymers, which determines the energy required for the crosspolymerization of diacetylene segments in the DA-polyesters, would therefore give rise to differences in the solid-state reactivity.
Wide-angle X-ray diffraction patterns of the DApolyesters HS, HI, HT, and OT(2) are shown in Figure 4.

It can be seen from Figure 4 and Table IV that the aliphatic DA-polyester HS shows three narrow and close crystalline peaks in shorter interchain spacing of 3–4 Å, indicating a more favorable structure for crosspolymerization.
Comparing meta- and para-isomers of aromatic DA-polyesters, i.e., HI and HT, a higher degree of crystallinity is observed in HI as the diffraction peaks are sharper with a lower amorphous background.

In fact, similar phenomena were reported for the diacetylene single-crystal systems where para-isomers were found to have larger interchain spacing compared to the meta-disubstituted counterparts.<sup>26,27</sup> Comparing the two para-disubstituted DA-polyesters, HT and OT(2), the diffraction peaks detected at higher 2u angle have very similar d-spacing (3.46 Å), but the interchain spacing of the lower 2u angle peak is found to be much larger for OT(2), 5.57 Å than that for HT, 4.46 Å.

It can be seen that aromatic DA-polyesters, HT, HI, and OT(2), are much more thermally stable than aliphatic DA-polyester HS, regardless of the testing atmosphere, due to the introduction of the benzene ring in the polymer backbone.

It is interesting to see that, for all DApolyesters studied in this work, the degradation occurred in two stages in air, leaving little or no residue, whereas the degradation occurred mainly in a single stage in nitrogen (200–500°C), leaving a considerable amount of residue of about 30–40%.

The DSC curves of as-synthesised DA-polyesters HS, HI, HT, and OT(2) are shown in Figure 5, and the temperatures of melting $( T _ { m } )$and exothermic reaction $( T _ { \mathrm { e x o } } )$of as-synthesised DA-polyesters and their enthalpies are summarized in Table VI.
This would enable these DA-polyesters to be processed in the melt state before a significant degree of crosspolymerization occurs.

It is important to point out the difference between the reactivity of the diacetylene units in the solid state and that in the molten state for these DApolyesters because only the former is believed to be controlled by the molecular packing geometry.

transition and the exothermic crosspolymerizating reaction (in the melt state) are more separated mainly because of the highly flexible aliphatic polymer chains in HS and the presence of the methyl side groups in OT(2).

It can also be seen from the DSC curves in Figure 5 that both aliphatic HS and meta-disubstituted HI exhibit a well-defined sharp single exothermic peak, while para-disubstituted HT and OT(2) give a much broader exothermic transition with two poorly defined peaks.

The solid-state crosspolymerization reactivity of these DA-polyesters was studied using the Raman technique on the isothermally treated DApolyesters, as discussed earlier.

No exothermic peaks were observed in the isothermal DSC traces even after 45 h at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for the aromatic DA-polyesters, although Raman spectra indicated partial crosspolymerization in HT and HI, as seen earlier in Figure 3.
However, the isothermal DSC trace at the same temperature shows a large distinct exotherm of 410 J/g, which peaks at 165 min, for the aliphatic HS, as seen in Figure 6.
Solution-cast films and melt processed OT(2) sheets were analyzed using DMA in tension mode and single-cantilever mode, respectively.

The beige-colored translucent HT films, typically 40 m thick, were cast from m-cresol, while the light-yellow color transparent OT(2) sheets, typically 1 mm thick, were obtained from melt processing of the as-synthesized OT(2) at ${ \bf 1 7 0 ^ { \circ } C }$DMA tests were also carried out on the heattreated samples to observe the effect of crosspolymerization.
It can be seen that the as-processed DApolyesters have unique dynamic mechanical behavior.
The initial large decrease in storage modulus $( E ^ { \prime } )$due to glass transition is followed by an equally large increase in $E ^ { \prime }$as the temperature rises for both HT and OT(2).

This increase in $E ^ { \prime }$is caused by the thermally initiated crosspolymerization that stiffens the polymer by introducing crosslinking and also by forming more rigid polydiacetylene chain reinforcing the polyester at the molecular level.

The results also show that, compared to OT(2) samples of the same thermal history, HT has a higher $T _ { g }$and a higher storage modulus value probably due to the absence of methyl side groups on this aromatic DA-polyester.
Substantial increases in the storage moduli of both HT and OT(2) were observed after thermal treatment, which should be due to crosspolymerization of DA-polyesters.

Attempts have been made to cast films from the m-cresol solutions of the polymers, and it was found that HT can be readily cast into compact and good-quality translucent films with a light beige color.
The measurements of the intrinsic viscosities were made in a thermostat bath regulated to 25 ± 0.02 °C. The dilute solution in m-cresol was charged into a Ubbelohde-type viscometer for testing.

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed using a TA Instruments of Hi-res TGA 2950 Thermogravimetric Analyzer. A sample of about 20 mg was put into a clean platinum pan and run under both nitrogen and air atmosphere from room temperature to 800 °C at a heating rate of 10°C/min.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was carried out employing a Perkin–Elmer DSC-7. All DA-polyesters were analyzed from 40 to 250°C under nitrogen purge at the heating rate of 10°C/min.

Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) data were collected through a TA Instruments Dynamic Mechanical Analyzer 2980. The measurement was performed at a heating rate of 3°C/min and a frequency of 1 Hz in air. The peak tan d temperature is taken as the glass transition temperature Tg.
